summary_md: Watkins and Dayan (Machine Learning 8, 1992, pp. 279-292) give the convergence proof for one-step Q-learning, a model-free way to learn optimal action values in a finite controlled Markov process. The theorem (p.282) says Q_n(x,a) converges to Q*(x,a) with probability 1 if rewards are bounded, learning rates sit in (0,1) with divergent sums and finite sums of squares, values are kept in a lookup table, and every state-action pair is tried infinitely often. The proof builds an artificial action-replay process from the episode history. Lemma A shows Q_n is optimal for that process. Lemma B shows the process converges to the real one. Section 4 sketches two extensions: undiscounted problems with absorbing goal states, and updating many Q values per step. It also notes that replaying stored episodes moves the method toward certainty-equivalence planning. The proof gives no convergence rate and no finite-sample bound. It does not cover function approximation, which the authors say may fail to converge (p.282), or multi-step TD(lambda) updates. For Paul's systems this is background rather than a method in use. The repo has no reinforcement learning. The joint optimizer is a certainty-equivalence planner. It takes a modeled stance state and runs exact greedy allocation over it, and its list for observed outcomes is empty. The paper matters for one point: Paul expects a learned policy such as GCOMB to replace greedy allocation at scale. GCOMB and S2V-DQN use Q-learning with function approximation, which is outside this theorem. A lobbying cycle also cannot try each member-action pair the many times the theorem requires. An online scan found no applications of RL to lobbying or to allocating contributions across legislators.

bearings.paper_claim: The convergence guarantee requires lookup-table action values and infinitely many trials of every state-action pair (p.281-282). The authors say Q-learning may not converge correctly with other representations (p.282) and give no rate or finite-sample bound. Section 4 (p.286) puts planning on a fixed sample (certainty equivalence) at the far end of a continuum with Q-learning. Citing Barto and Singh (1990), it says acting as if an early model were accurate costs dearly early in learning (p.280).
bearings.paper_location: Section 2 pp.280-282 (theorem and conditions); Section 4 p.286 (certainty-equivalence continuum)
bearings.system_side: The optimizer allocates a 2.5M pot in 500-dollar chunks by lazy greedy over a modeled, fixed stance state. Its docstring says the result is exact only in that state. It is pure certainty-equivalence planning with no learning. The observations list is reserved for real outcomes and stays empty. Threshold conversions are modeled transitions that trigger replanning, not observed rewards. Paul's position expects a learned policy (GCOMB) to replace greedy at scale.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The theorem holds only for a finite MDP with repeated sampled transitions and lookup-table values. One election cycle across 533 members yields at most a few observed outcomes per member-action pair, so the infinite-sampling condition cannot be met. Learned policies in the GCOMB and S2V-DQN family use Q-learning with function approximation and fall outside the theorem entirely. At the current problem size, exact greedy is already optimal in a fixed state, so a learned policy has nothing to gain on that point.

bearings.paper_claim: Q-learning learns action values from sampled rewards without a model, but only as each state-action pair is sampled without bound. The action-replay estimates of rewards and transitions converge with probability 1 only as the number of samples grows to infinity (Lemma B.3, pp.284, 290).
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1 Lemma B.3 p.284; Appendix p.290
bearings.system_side: SGATE is a fixed hand-set take-up table by stance tier: Highly Persuadable 1.00 down to Opponent 0.35, unknown 0.85. It is multiplied by the receptivity seed_prob with a floor of 0.15. Paul ties it to Chen et al. 2021, which is RL-based contingency-aware seeding. The built gate is a fixed prior, not a learned value, and nothing updates it from observed contact outcomes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Learning take-up rates the way Q-learning learns values would need repeated observed contact-to-action outcomes per tier. The system does not have that log at present. The paper gives no finite-sample rate, so it cannot say how many observations would be enough.

gaps_exposed: No observed-outcome feedback loop: optimize.py keeps an empty observations list, so every allocation is certainty-equivalence planning on modeled stance states. No sampled rewards ever update the model.
SGATE take-up probabilities and PERS tiers are fixed priors. Nothing estimates them from logged contact outcomes, so no learning method (RL or otherwise) has data to work from.
The allocator is single-cycle and one-shot. No multi-cycle sequential policy is modeled, which would be the setting where an MDP framing such as Q-learning applies.

Paul's expectation that a learned policy (GCOMB) replaces greedy at scale has no stated convergence or sample-size basis. The tabular guarantee in this paper does not carry over to function-approximation Q-learning.
paul_alignment: Paul has no entry or markup for this work. His nearest position is that a learned policy (GCOMB) should replace greedy allocation at scale. This paper qualifies that: the guarantee covers only lookup-table Q-learning with unbounded sampling. GCOMB uses function approximation, which may not converge (p.282). The built optimizer is a greedy planner that is exact in a fixed modeled state (optimize.py:3-12). So the replacement is a scaling preference, not a convergence-backed upgrade. The position is not stale, since no learned policy exists, but this source does not support it.

related.why: Textbook treatment of Q-learning as off-policy TD control. It covers the deadly triad (function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy learning), which explains where this paper's tabular guarantee stops.

GCOMB trains its node-selection policy with Q-learning over GCN embeddings for budget-constrained influence maximization. That is function-approximation Q-learning, outside this theorem, and it is the learned policy Paul expects to replace greedy allocation.

S2V-DQN learns greedy graph heuristics with n-step fitted Q-learning on graph embeddings. It extends this paper's update to multi-step returns and function approximation, two cases this paper says its proof does not cover.
Contingency-aware influence maximization trained with reinforcement learning. It is the source Paul maps onto SGATE, and its learning step descends from the Q-learning update proved here.
Applies deep RL, a Q-learning descendant, to influence maximization under complex contagion. That is the threshold-adoption setting closest to the system's linear-threshold priming.
Uses deep reinforcement learning to choose edge activations for influence maximization. It is a function-approximation descendant of Q-learning with no tabular convergence guarantee.

An alternative to RL for sequential decisions under uncertainty. Adaptive greedy comes with an approximation guarantee and needs no asymptotic sampling. The joint optimizer keeps its data-dependent bound as a diagnostic.
